hints: Look closely at line X. It stays well above $0$ kPa for the whole $0.8$ s, while the other two lines fall back to near zero in diastole. Which right-side structure keeps its pressure up even when the heart is relaxing?

Remember the difference between a ventricle and a great artery. The ventricle pressure must fall to near zero to allow filling, but the artery stays pressurised because its semilunar valve shuts and its elastic wall recoils.
walkthrough:
**Observe what X does**

Look at the solid line labelled X. It starts relatively high, dips a little at about $0.2$ s, then rises slightly and stays high, slowly falling but never reaching zero.

The other two lines both drop to around $0$ kPa for much of the cycle.

**Recall pressures on the right side**

On the right side we have: vena cava and right atrium with very low pressure (close to $0$ kPa), right ventricle with a big sharp rise during systole then a fall to near zero in diastole, and pulmonary artery which receives the blood.

Key rule: ventricular pressure falls low in diastole to allow filling, arterial pressure stays up.

**Match X to the pulmonary artery**

The tall dashed peak that shoots up at $0.2$ s and crashes down at $0.45$ s is the right ventricle contracting and then relaxing.

Line X follows the ventricle up a little (when the valve opens and blood is ejected) but then stays high when the ventricle falls. That maintained pressure with a small dicrotic bump is classic for an artery, here the pulmonary artery.

options.A: Correct. X maintains a pressure above zero throughout, rising during ventricular systole and showing elastic recoil afterwards. That is exactly the pulmonary artery.
options.B: Not correct. The right atrium has very low pressure near $0$ kPa with only tiny waves, shown by the small dotted line, not the high sustained line X.
options.C: Not correct. The right ventricle shows the large dashed peak in systole but its pressure falls to near zero in diastole to allow filling, so it cannot be the sustained high line X.
options.D: Not correct. The vena cava, like the atrium, is at very low pressure close to $0$ kPa throughout, not the much higher pressure of X.
